clue.text: Coffee back in canteen, provided cups laid out (9)

indicators.note: The back of a word is its far end, so canteen gives up only the letter it finishes on.
A cup holds whatever is put in it, so the piece named beside it closes right around the others.

blocks.note: to provide for someone is to feed them; three letters that will be opened up
the milky coffee everyone orders, five letters going straight in
the letter at the back of the word canteen, the one it ends on

explanation.surface: Coffee goes back to the canteen, where the cups have been set out ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid out' reads as a line about table settings, which is what the canteen and the cups are for, and it is the boxing sense instead. Providing for someone is feeding them.
explanation.definitionFit: laid out → FLATTENED: a boxer laid out on the canvas has been flattened, the knocked-flat sense rather than the neatly-arranged one.

clue.text: Flounce and kick down Whitechapel Road? (5)

indicators.note: Whitechapel Road runs through London's East End, so the word is being said in a Cockney accent, and an opening 'th' comes out of a Cockney mouth as an 'f'.

blocks.note: a kick is a thrill, the jolt of excitement you get from something
say that word in the East End and the 'th' becomes an 'f', which is spelt differently

explanation.surface: Someone storms off, aiming a kick as they go down an East End street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flounce' reads as the verb, somebody stomping away in a huff, and it is the noun: a strip of gathered fabric. Whitechapel Road names an accent, not a place in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flounce → FRILL: a flounce is the gathered strip of material sewn round a skirt, which is exactly what a frill is.

clue.text: See 21 Across
Leader on laptop behind it, our chats fallacious? (5,6)

definitions.text: Leader on laptop behind it, our chats fallacious?

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter it starts on, so laptop hands over its opening letter and nothing else.
Whatever is behind the rest comes last, so that single letter waits at the end of the assembly.
What is fallacious cannot be trusted, and letters you cannot trust are not standing in the order they were handed to you.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, taken from three ordinary words
the letter laptop leads with, dropped in at the back of the queue

explanation.surface: A politician sits behind a laptop while the conversations the rest of us have there turn out to be untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs: read straight the sentence describes the site, and read as instructions 'Leader' stops being a politician and becomes the letter laptop starts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes Donald Trump's own network: he is behind it, the posts there are notoriously untrue, and the name says the opposite.

clue.text: Hardly what conductor may seemingly have done with it (3,1,3)

indicators.note: A conductor's stick spends the whole concert being waved around, so whatever he seemingly did with it leaves those letters in no fixed order.

blocks.note: the slim stick a conductor holds; the clue wants the thing, not the man
the clue's own two letters join the fodder as they stand

explanation.surface: A conductor appears to have done something peculiar with his baton.
explanation.walkthrough: The word to shuffle is never written down: 'conductor' asks you to supply the stick yourself before there are any letters to work with. 'Hardly' is the definition, tucked in at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardly → NOT A BIT: 'did you mind? Not a bit' is a flat denial, the same as saying you hardly minded at all.

clue.text: Triggered by old boarding school? On the contrary (9)

indicators.note: Boarding a train is climbing inside it, so one piece goes in among the letters of another.
It tells you the two pieces swap roles: what looked like the passenger turns out to be the vehicle.

blocks.note: a dated jacket is an old one; five letters that open up to let something in
Eton, the boarding school near Windsor, is the school crosswords reach for first

explanation.surface: Somebody is set off by memories of the boarding school they were sent to years ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as it stands, the old thing climbs into the school; 'On the contrary' turns that round, so the school goes inside the old one. Being 'triggered' is the modern sense of a very old word.
explanation.definitionFit: Triggered → DETONATED: a charge that has been triggered has gone off, the literal explosive sense sitting underneath today's figurative one.

clue.text: See 20 Down
Upbringing happy, good day to hide – nowhere to disappear? (4,3)

indicators.note: Bringing something up a down clue writes it from the bottom towards the top, so those letters arrive back to front.
Hiding a thing puts it out of sight inside something bigger, and the letters already assembled are the hiding place.

blocks.note: riant is a word for cheerful, borrowed from the French for laughing, and here it is read upwards
the greeting you give someone, two letters, tucked into the middle

explanation.surface: Someone remembers a happy childhood, then decides today is a good day to keep out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upbringing' reads as a noun about childhood and is really an instruction: in a down clue, bringing letters up means writing them from the bottom. Riant is rare enough to be worth keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: nowhere to disappear? → THIN AIR: things that vanish are said to vanish into thin air, the idiom's name for the nowhere they go to.

clue.text: Clear I am at home when opening lift (9)

indicators.note: To open something is to make a gap in it, and the gap is where the other letters are pushed in.

blocks.note: to lift someone's spirits is to elate them; five letters about to be prised apart
I am shortened to I'm, with the apostrophe dropped
someone at home is in, the crossword's most-used two letters

explanation.surface: Someone announces that they are indoors just as the lift doors open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' wants to be the elevator the surface is standing in, and it is the verb: to lift someone is to elate them. 'At home' for IN is worth learning once and keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear → ELIMINATE: clearing a room of people is getting rid of them, and getting rid of something altogether is what the verb means.

clue.text: One’s filled with various pictures (3,5)

indicators.note: Various things differ from one another, so the letters beside it are not to be taken in the arrangement shown.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, and the enumeration splits them three and five

explanation.surface: An album or a frame is filled with an assortment of photographs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pictures' wants to be the definition — the cinema, a wall of photographs — and it is the letters. What gets filled here is pastry, and the clue never says so.
explanation.definitionFit: One’s filled → PIE CRUST: the pastry case is the thing a filling goes into, so the clue names it by the job it does.

clue.text: Rat, I suspect, has gobbled six trifles (6)

indicators.note: Something suspect is not what it claims to be, and neither is the order these four letters claim.
To gobble is to swallow whole, so the letters in front close over the piece that follows.

blocks.note: four letters shaken up before anything is let inside them
six written as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A rat is suspected of having eaten six trifles from the fridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifles' is the definition, and the surface makes it the pudding a rat would go for. The sense wanted is the other one: things too small to matter.
explanation.definitionFit: trifles → TRIVIA: trivia are the small unimportant details of a subject, exactly what trifles means when it is not a dessert.

clue.text: Shed in Berkshire town (6)

blocks.note: the verb a snake performs on its old skin, casting it off whole
the town west of London on the road out to Windsor, in the county of Berkshire

explanation.surface: Something has been shed somewhere in a town in Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are said differently — the verb rhymes with 'rough', the town with 'plough' — which is how the join passes as one ordinary sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Shed → SLOUGH: a snake sloughs its skin, and the same spelling names the Berkshire town John Betjeman wrote his rudest poem about.

clue.text: US author referencing issue with mountain, page covered by explanation for sticky foot? (8,5)

indicators.note: Something covered by another thing lies underneath it, out of sight, so that single letter is buried inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: ben is the Scottish word for a mountain — Ben Nevis is the highest of them
jam in a sock would certainly account for a foot that sticks, and the three words are taken exactly as they read
p is the standard abbreviation for page, the one used in footnotes

explanation.surface: An American writer is cited alongside a mountain and a page explaining how somebody's foot got sticky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is the old word for offspring, and that is what this doctor's famous book was about — so the definition describes the man rather than just naming his nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: US author referencing issue → BENJAMIN SPOCK: 'issue' means children, and his Baby and Child Care told American parents how to bring theirs up.

clue.text: Rubbish charges thus frozen (6)

indicators.note: You charge a glass by filling it, so the word in front is packed inside the piece that follows.

blocks.note: sic is Latin for thus, the word bracketed into a quotation to show it is copied exactly
tat is British for cheap worthless stuff, the junk at the end of a market stall

explanation.surface: A council headline: the charges for taking rubbish away have been held at last year's price.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a headline, 'charges' is what the council bills you and 'frozen' is what happens to a fee. The instruction hiding inside it is the other charging, filling a glass to the brim.
explanation.definitionFit: frozen → STATIC: something frozen has stopped moving, and static means standing still, nothing to do with the cold.

clue.text: Subject of pop artist put on, if so surrealistic? (3,2,4)

indicators.note: A surrealist painting puts familiar things in impossible arrangements, which is what has happened to these letters.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, and the enumeration breaks them three, two and four

explanation.surface: A gallery-goer wonders whether the pop artist's chosen subject, once hung, counts as surreal.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop art's most famous subject is Andy Warhol's Campbell's cans, silkscreened over and over. Surrealism is a different movement altogether, which is why the word passes as description.
explanation.definitionFit: Subject of pop artist → TIN OF SOUP: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans made a supermarket tin the most painted object of the movement.

clue.text: Vessel requiring a load gets it on (9)

blocks.note: a tin is a vessel, three letters for the thing the beans come in
oodles of something is loads of it

explanation.surface: A ship that needs cargo aboard before it can get going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' is placed to look like a ship waiting for its load, and the tin on the shelf is the one wanted. The definition is the modern phrase for a couple getting amorous.
explanation.definitionFit: gets it on → CANOODLES: to canoodle is to cuddle and kiss, the affectionate end of what 'getting it on' covers.

clue.text: Class nuisance, out unfortunately for detention (8)

indicators.note: When things fall out unfortunately they do not land where they were meant to, and neither do these letters.

blocks.note: a trial is a person or thing that wears you down — 'that child is a trial'
the clue's own three letters join the fodder as they stand
surface only: it says where the nuisance is being sent and hands over no letters

explanation.surface: A disruptive pupil is sent out of the room and given detention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class nuisance' reads as one phrase, the pest at the back of the room, and the setter has cut it in half: the first word is the definition and the second is letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Class → TUTORIAL: a tutorial is a teaching session for one student or a few, so it is a class in the sense of a lesson.

clue.text: Red upset with union awaiting the press? (8)

indicators.note: Upsetting something tips its contents out anyhow, so the letters land in an order of their own.

blocks.note: three letters of fodder, sitting in front of the instruction
five more letters of fodder, taken exactly as spelt

explanation.surface: An angry socialist has fallen out with his union and is waiting for the newspapers to call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The press' is journalists all the way through the surface — a Red at odds with his union is a front page — and the definition wants the household appliance instead.
explanation.definitionFit: awaiting the press? → UNIRONED: a shirt still waiting for the iron has not been pressed, so the press here is the flat hot one.

clue.text: Breather touching on venom (7)

blocks.note: re means on the subject of, the word at the head of a memo
spite is venom in the figurative sense, the poison in what somebody says

explanation.surface: A short break in an argument that keeps circling back to something poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breather' looks like the thing doing the breathing — a creature, a diver — and it is the pause you take. The venom is not a snake's but the human kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Breather → RESPITE: a breather is a short pause to get your breath back, and respite is that same pause seen as relief.

clue.text: A shipmate’s last race having capsized on the ocean (4-3)

indicators.note: The last of a word is the letter it ends on, so shipmate gives up its final letter alone.
A capsized boat has turned right over, and in a down clue that means these letters are read from the bottom up.

blocks.note: the clue's first word, one letter taken as it stands
the letter shipmate ends on
to race along is to speed; these five join the two above before the whole lot goes over

explanation.surface: A sailor's final race ends with the boat going over in open water.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole sentence reads as a sailing report, which is how 'capsized' passes for narrative rather than the instruction it is. The answer is the adjective, as in deep-sea fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: on the ocean → DEEP-SEA: deep-sea fishing and deep-sea diving both happen far out on the open ocean rather than off the shore.

clue.text: Twitter feed, it heralding gulps? (6)

indicators.note: To gulp is to swallow something whole, and a word swallowed by its neighbours is sitting inside them unbroken.

blocks.note: run the three words together and six consecutive letters, starting three in, are the ones wanted

explanation.surface: A social-media feed that seems to be announcing a series of nervous swallows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitter' is the old noun here: being all of a twitter is being in a flutter of nerves. The birdsong and the website are both decoys, and so is reading 'gulps' as a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Twitter → DITHER: to be in a twitter and to be in a dither name the same jittery state, unable to settle or decide.

clue.text: Skeleton with less foot to shake about, scintillating dancer? (11)

indicators.note: The foot of a word in a down clue is the letter at the bottom of it, and 'less' throws that letter away.
Shake a thing about and nothing stays where it started, so the letters are rebuilt in any order you like.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, taken whole
the word WITH loses the letter at its foot, leaving three to join the pile

explanation.surface: A skeleton missing a foot gets rattled about, and out comes a dazzling dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' does two jobs: the bone the skeleton has lost in the picture, and the bottom letter of a word in the instruction. Down clues can talk about tops and feet because they run vertically.
explanation.definitionFit: scintillating dancer? → TWINKLE TOES: twinkletoes is what you call someone light and quick on their feet, and to twinkle is to scintillate.

clue.text: A less taxing sailors’ yarn? (8,7)

blocks.note: the surface promises something easier going; the other reading is literal, money parked where the taxman cannot reach it
a yarn is a story, and the story a sailor tells is told out at sea, well away from the shore

explanation.surface: An old salt spins a tall tale that is easier going than most of his.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taxing' swings between two meanings: demanding, and to do with tax. Once it lands on the second, the sailors stop being storytellers and start meaning anything out beyond the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A less taxing sailors’ yarn? → OFFSHORE ACCOUNT: an account is a yarn, and offshore is both out at sea and safely out of the taxman's reach.

clue.text: Ticked off – as top? (6)

definitions.note: The second definition is a joke formation: it asks for an adjective built out of a word for a top, which is not a use the dictionary records.

blocks.note: the slang sense: annoyed, needled, in a huff about something
like a particular kind of top — the one with a collar and cuffs — with a -y stuck on the end

explanation.surface: A telling-off, followed by a question about somebody's choice of top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ticked off' has three senses — crossed off a list, told off, annoyed — and only the last one fits. The second half is the setter building an adjective out of a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticked off → SHIRTY: it is the annoyed sense, and 'as top?' reads the same word as shirt-like, which is where the adjective came from.

clue.text: See 11 Across
Principle, if flipping the same? (5)

indicators.note: A word that is the same when flipped reads identically from either end, so there is nothing to turn round — only the symmetry to spot.

blocks.note: the definition end of the clue: a belief held as a rule to live or work by
the wordplay end: five letters reading the same from either direction, which is all the help on offer

explanation.walkthrough: Five letters that read the same both ways is the whole of the wordplay. Christopher Nolan named a film after this word for exactly that symmetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Principle → TENET: a tenet is a principle held as an article of belief, the sort a party or a faith is built on.

clue.text: See 3 Down
Odious pipe, with joint to inhale (8)

indicators.note: Inhaling draws something right inside you, so the piece named goes into the middle of the other one.

blocks.note: to pipe up is to sing out; four letters about to be opened
the hock is the joint in an animal's hind leg, and a hock of ham is the cut around it

explanation.surface: A revolting pipe is passed round along with a joint to smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all smoking — a pipe, a joint, inhaling — and not one of those senses is wanted. The joint comes from a butcher, and to pipe is to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Odious → SHOCKING: something odious gives offence, and shocking is that offence at full strength, as in 'shocking behaviour'.

clue.text: Recess, politicians on vacation in Adelaide spewing guts (4)

indicators.note: A word on vacation is emptied out like a house for the summer, keeping only the letters at either end.
Being in a place is being inside it, so that pair of letters sits within the pair that follows.
Spewing your guts is bringing up everything inside, so the middle of the word goes and the outsides stay.

blocks.note: the Australian city keeps only its first and last letters once the middle is gone
the word politicians emptied of everything between its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Politicians on holiday in Adelaide are being noisily sick.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words are hollowed out by the same trick, and the clue says it twice in different language: one goes on holiday, the other is sick. Both keep nothing but their outsides.
explanation.definitionFit: Recess → APSE: an apse is the vaulted recess at the east end of a church, so this is the architectural sense of the word.

clue.text: Short continental break where plonk guzzled – and most bubbly? (9)

indicators.note: Short means cut off before the end, so the word beside it arrives one letter light.
It marks the spot: the place named next sits inside the word that has just been shortened.

blocks.note: the afternoon nap taken all over southern Europe, with its final letter cut off
cheap wine gets drunk out of doors, and the public park is where that happens

explanation.surface: A quick holiday in Europe where the cheap wine goes down fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continental break' reads as a weekend in Europe, and the break wanted is the one Spain takes after lunch. 'Most' belongs to the definition, supplying its superlative ending.
explanation.definitionFit: most bubbly? → SPARKIEST: a sparky person fizzes with energy, and the superlative picks out the one who bubbles most of all.
